title: Chain length effects on molecular interaction between octanal + 1-alkanol (C3–C7) mixture: thermophysical measurements and quantum chemical insights
content: The relationship between molecular interactions and macroscopic thermophysical properties is important for understanding the behavior of non-ideal liquid mixtures. This study investigates the effect of alcohol chain length on the thermophysical properties and intermolecular interactions of binary mixtures of octanal (Oct) with 1-alkanols ranging from 1-propanol to 1-heptanol (C3–C7). Here, alcohol use refers solely to the 1-alkanols as mixture components. Experimental density and viscosity measurements were used to determine the excess molar volume (VE) and the viscosity deviation (Δη) via the Redlich–Kister equation. Complementary quantum chemical calculations investigated the isolated Oct–alcohol complexes and their electronic properties were investigated using quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM), electrostatic molecular potential (ESP), frontier molecular orbitals and electron localization analyses. The experimental results show a systematic change in thermophysical behavior with increasing alcohol chain length. The excess molar volumes are negative for mixtures of 1-propanol with 1-pentanol, but positive for the 1-hexanol and 1-heptanol systems. Similarly, the viscosity deviations are positive for C3–C5 and negative for C6–C7. The calculated raw interaction energies corrected by the repulsion force become progressively more negative from C3 to C7, indicating an increasing stabilization of the isolated molecular pairs. Electronic structure analyses consistently identify the O–H⋯O═  C contact as the main interaction motif. To further understand the organization of the bulk liquid phase, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed, and the derived radial distribution functions (RDFs) confirm that the structured hydrogen-bonding network at C3 is significantly disrupted by the steric hindrance at C7, reducing the packing efficiency of the liquid phase. These findings suggest that the interaction energies of the lone pairs do not directly determine the signs of excess molar volume or viscosity deviation. Rather, the experimental trends reflect the bulk behavior of the liquid mixtures, in which molecular connectivity, dispersion interactions, and compaction effects may all play a role. Combined experimental and computational results provide complementary insights into the relationship between molecular structure and thermophysical behavior in octanal–alcohol mixtures.
